props.title: Heroes

sections.content: **Heroes** (2006) revolutionized superhero television by grounding extraordinary abilities in ordinary lives. Following **Lost** (2004) and **24** (2001), it captured peak serialized TV storytelling with its "save the cheerleader, save the world" hook. Creator Tim Kring wove together a sprawling ensemble cast, with Masi Oka's time-bending Hiro Nakamura and Zachary Quinto's menacing Sylar emerging as breakout characters. The show's first season masterfully built tension through interconnected storylines, much like **Watchmen** (2019) would later do for HBO.

sections.content: The show's DNA traces back to **X-Men** (2000), which proved superhero stories could balance character drama with special effects. Like **Misfits** (2009) and **The Umbrella Academy** (2019), Heroes explored how sudden powers affect dysfunctional family dynamics and personal relationships. The series particularly excelled in its first season's tight plotting and character work, though later seasons struggled to maintain that quality - a common challenge also faced by **Lost** (2004) and **Alias** (2001).

Heroes' visual style influenced countless superhero shows that followed. **The Tomorrow People** (2013) and **The Gifted** (2017) adopted similar approaches to depicting powers on a TV budget. The series also helped establish the template for interconnected superhero narratives on television, paving the way for The CW's Arrowverse and Marvel's Netflix shows like **Daredevil** (2015). sections.content: While Heroes' quality declined in later seasons, its impact on television superhero stories remains significant. Shows like **The Boys** (2019) and **Invincible** (2021) build on its foundation of examining how superpowers affect ordinary people and society. The series also helped launch careers, with Zachary Quinto going on to **Star Trek** (2009) and Milo Ventimiglia starring in **This Is Us** (2016).
